Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Houston Astros shortstop Miguel Tejada is expected to plead guilty Wednesday in federal court to a count of lying to Congress about his knowledge of Major League Baseball players using performance-enhancing drugs, according to officials familiar with the case. Miguel Tejada, a shortstop for the Houston Astros, has been charged with lying to Congress. In a document filed in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, Tejada is charged in a criminal "information," a document that routinely signals a plea bargain agreement. The document does not directly accuse Tejada of using steroids or other substances. However, the court document says that in 2003 Tejada gave another player more than $5,000 in checks "for substances which he believed to be HGH [human growth hormone]." The document says Tejada lied to congressional investigators when he told them on August 26, 2005, that he had never heard discussions about steroids by other players, and that he never knew of any other player using steroids. After the December 2007 Mitchell Report on steroid use in baseball, which appeared to contradict Tejada, the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform asked the Justice Department to investigate whether Tejada "made knowingly false statements to the committee." The investigators concluded he had lied. "Defendant Tejada unlawfully withheld pertinent information from the committee because defendant Tejada before and during his interview with the committee staff, then and there well knew that Player #1 [unidentified], one of his teammates on the Oakland Athletics, had used steroids and HGH," the document says. Tejada played for the Athletics from 1997 to 2003. He is scheduled to appear at 11 a.m. Wednesday before a magistrate judge, indicating the charge against him will be a misdemeanor carrying a maximum sentence of a year in jail. However, a government official familiar with the case said that under sentencing guidelines, Tejada could get from zero to 6 months, which means he may receive probation without jail time. Tejada, who started his MLB career in 1997, hit at least 30 home runs from 2000 through 2004 with the exception of 2003, when he hit 27. He won the American League's most valuable player award in 2002, when he hit a career-best 34 home runs. He matched that total in 2004, his first year with the Baltimore Orioles. He began playing with Houston in 2008. The information came one day after MLB star Alex Rodriguez -- the New York Yankees' third baseman since 2004 -- admitted that he had used a "banned substance" during the 2001-2003 seasons. Sports Illustrated had reported that Rodriguez had tested positive for steroids in 2003, when he was playing for the Texas Rangers.

## Objective Report: Miguel Tejada’s Charge, the HGH/“Player #1” Filing, and the Alex Rodriguez Connection

Miguel Tejada, a former American League Most Valuable Player, was charged in 2009 with lying to Congress in connection with baseball’s performance-enhancing drug investigations. The charge arose from statements he made to congressional investigators in 2005, when he was questioned about steroid use in Major League Baseball.

### Why Tejada Was Charged

Tejada was charged with making false statements to congressional investigators. Prosecutors said he was not charged with using steroids or human growth hormone, but with giving misleading answers during an official inquiry.

According to the criminal information filed in federal court, Tejada told investigators that he had no knowledge of other players using or discussing steroids or HGH. Prosecutors alleged that those statements were false because Tejada had, in fact, had conversations with another player about performance-enhancing drugs.

The filing said Tejada denied knowing about steroid use and denied having relevant discussions with other players, even though investigators believed he possessed information that was important to Congress’s inquiry into drug use in baseball.

### What the Court Filing Says About HGH Checks and “Player #1”

The court filing referred to another baseball player only as “Player #1.” That player was described as someone who had discussed steroids and HGH with Tejada.

The filing said that in 2003, Tejada gave Player #1 checks that were connected to the purchase of human growth hormone. Reports at the time identified the checks as totaling about $6,300. The filing stated that Player #1 had obtained HGH and that Tejada had knowledge of discussions about performance-enhancing substances.

However, the charge against Tejada did not require prosecutors to prove that he personally used HGH or steroids. The legal issue was whether he lied when he told congressional investigators that he had no knowledge of such drug use or conversations.

### Relation to Alex Rodriguez’s Steroid Admission

Tejada’s case emerged during the same broader period of public and legal scrutiny over steroid use in Major League Baseball. It came shortly after Alex Rodriguez admitted that he had used performance-enhancing drugs while playing for the Texas Rangers from 2001 to 2003.

The two matters were not the same case, and Rodriguez’s admission did not cause Tejada’s charge. But they were linked by the larger context: congressional investigations, the Mitchell Report, and increasing public attention to baseball’s “steroid era.”

Rodriguez’s admission reinforced the extent of performance-enhancing drug use among prominent players during that period, while Tejada’s case showed that legal consequences could arise not only from alleged drug use itself, but also from false or misleading statements made to federal investigators or Congress.
